CHAPTER 3 
STATUTES OF FRAUDS 
SECTION 1. 
INTRODUCTION 
When we use the word contract, we commonly have two different 
things in mind. One is the somewhat abstract idea of an enforceable 
promise, to paraphrase Restatement 
§ 1. The other is a document that 
embodies that promise. (Note that the UCC definition of "contract" in 
UCC § 1-20l(b)(12) covers only the former.) As we have seen, however, a 
promise generally n ed not be in writing to be enforced; consider 
Hawkins v. McGee and Sullivan v. O'Connor, for example. 
Just because oral promises may be enforceable does not mean that 
it is a good idea to make one's promises orally. True, even huge contracts 
are sealed with .1 handshake. But oral promises are subject to the 
memories of those who made them, memories that may fade or transmute 
with time--and whicl have been known to change in the face of a dispute. 
Over time, the t •rms of oral contracts may resemble 
the game of 
"Telephone," with a word whisper d at the start of a chain often coming 
out garbled at the md. 
The law thl'refore treats 
oral contracts and written contracts 
somewhat differently. One of the ways in which it does so concerns how 
the law determine~ what the terms of a written contract are and what 
they mean. This topic is discussed in Chapter 5. The other i more 
fundamental: whether the contract is enforceable at all. That is this 
chapter's subject. 
Whether oral 1·ontracts are enforceable is almost entirely governed 
by statutes, generically called "statutes of frauds" after the first of its 
kind, An Act for Pn:vention of Fraud and Perjuries, 29 Car. 2, c. 3 (1677).a 
The original Statute of Frauds listed six categories of contracts that 
would be enforceable only if in a signed writing: (1) a contract by an 
executor or admini, trator of an estate to answer for a duty of the 
decedent (the executor-administrator 
provision); (2) a contract to answer 
for the debt of another (the suretyship 
provision); (3) a contract made 
upon consideration of marriage (the marriage provision); (4) a contract 
for the sale of an interest in land (the land contract provision); (5) a 
contract that is not to be performed within one year of its making (the 
one-year provision); and (6) a contract for the sale of goods (the sale of 
goods provision). Nor are these the only writing requirements 
in the 
st~t~te books. In Professor Farnsworth's 
words, "legislators have an 
abiding faith in formality." Farnsworth 
on Contracts 
§ 6.2, at 110.
